Artificial Intelligence is the broad field. Machine Learning is a subset of AI — it is already in your life: fraud detection at Visa, Face ID, Netflix recommendations, Outlook spam filtering, Google Maps routing. contentBlocks.content: Option 1: Turn your idea into a prompt. Let Claude interview you.

contentBlocks.label: The interview prompt
contentBlocks.content:
You're going to help me plan an app I'm about to build with AI. I'm not a developer.

Interview me. Ask one question at a time and wait for my answer before asking the next. Keep your questions short and in plain English — no technical terms.

Work through these four things, in this order:

1. Who's allowed in, and how they get in
2. What people see and do when they open it
3. What rules it follows — what happens when someone does something
4. What it needs to remember between visits

If I don't know an answer, suggest something reasonable and move on. If my idea is getting too big, tell me and help me cut it down to the smallest version worth building.

When we're done, write me a short prompt I can paste into Replit. Write it as a person describing what they want — plain sentences, no bullet lists, no technical terms, no mention of databases or components. Six sentences or fewer.

Start by asking me what I want to build.
Option 2: Write it yourself — four fields, same four questions.

contentBlocks.content: The fix isn't better AI. It's a human in the loop. Beginning: you direct. Middle: AI processes. End: you edit and oversee it.

contentBlocks.title: The trap
contentBlocks.content: These systems perform trust. They don't earn it. The better they get at the performance, the harder it is to remember. Your job: understand it. Don't trust it.
Know the four parts, so you know where to look when something breaks.

contentBlocks.title: The takeaway
contentBlocks.content: Every app has four parts: a way in, an interface/experience, the rules, and storage. Knowing them helps you point to what's wrong when something breaks — most of the time, you just describe what you want and the AI figures out the rest.
Which of your real tasks suit the tools you actually have? Recurring, language-heavy work. Not anything the number has to be right on.

An agent is different. You hand it a goal. It decides what files to create, writes them, hits errors, reads the errors, fixes them, and keeps going until something ran. Their words went in. An agent did the rest.

An LLM predicts the next word based on massive training data. It's not retrieving a fixed answer; it's generating a likely sequence. When it lands on truth, we call it an answer. When it lands on false, we call it a hallucination. Same process either way. It doesn't know it's right. It doesn't know it's wrong. It's always guessing.
More context means better predictions. "Mary ___" could be anything. "Mary had a little ___" is almost certainly one word. Vague prompts get vague outputs. Your context is the lever.

contentBlocks.content: It's not laziness. It's misplaced confidence. Confidence in the tool lowers critical thinking; confidence in yourself raises it. Effort drops most at the judgment end — evaluation, synthesis, analysis. Tool first, thinking second: the order matters.

The failure is invisible until a decision goes wrong. Gradual drift: session one you edit, session three you copy-paste. Output homogenizes — the memos start sounding alike. "It wrote it" replaces "I wrote it." Skill loss shows up only when the tool is gone. Two or three people trusted the polish before it reached you.

contentBlocks.title: The takeaway
contentBlocks.content: Point the AI at something real — your website, your brand — and it gets closer. When it misses, add detail. More context in, better result out.
Beyond Copilot, Traffic Mobility Insight, and Road Safety Insight. Remember the three ways: Chat, Automate, Delegate.
Automate — the path is fixed, AI can live inside it
The workflow does not decide what happens next. You already did.

Delegate — the path is discovered while the work is happening. Example: "Prepare Monday's executive brief." The agent pulls the calendar, project data, email updates, and policy news, asks what's missing, searches an alternate source, synthesizes, drafts. The path changes when the evidence changes.
Some of the people you lead have used these tools. They know the gap.
Shadow AI is evidence. It tells leaders where capability, policy, and user need are out of alignment.

You did not choose it. Copilot arrived in an update — every M365 tenant got it. Gemini arrived in a browser patch that IT approved as a security fix. Connectors arrive through your own tools: an approved tool with an admin panel connects to anything. The question is not whether you have shadow AI. It is whether you can see it.
Read the signal — the workaround is telling you something

cards.body: The approved tool cannot do the job. People reach outside when the sanctioned option stops short.
cards.title: CAPABILITY

cards.body: The rules do not match the work. A blanket restriction collides with a legitimate operational need.
cards.title: POLICY

cards.body: People do not know the sanctioned path. The capability may exist; they just don't know how to reach it.
cards.title: ENABLEMENT

contentBlocks.content: Before you punish the workaround, diagnose the gap.

cards.body: Finds a person.
cards.title: "WHO IS USING UNAPPROVED AI?"

cards.body: Finds the gap.
cards.title: "WHAT ARE THEY TRYING TO ACCOMPLISH THAT THEY CANNOT ACCOMPLISH ANOTHER WAY?"

cards.body: Catch it. Stop it. People learn what not to tell you. The behavior gets harder to see, not less common.
cards.title: SURVEILLANCE

cards.body: See it. Understand it. Ask what the tool is doing for them. Visibility gives you something you can actually govern.
cards.title: SUNLIGHT

contentBlocks.content: Make the sanctioned path win. People choose the approved path when it gives them more, not merely when policy tells them to: approved data, shared prompts, internal knowledge, better integrations, reusable workflows. Compliance is not the incentive. Capability is.

contentBlocks.title: Trust but verify
contentBlocks.content: Enable, train, make the path known — that sets the direction and gets people to tell you what they use. Then check at machine speed. AI runs at machine speed, so the check on it has to.

Before we talk about AI safety, let's talk about data safety. Optimize entirely for efficiency and everything is wide open. Optimize entirely for safety and we'd never send an email. Every organization lives somewhere in the middle.
"Is this safe?" is not a question that has an answer. Safe compared to what? For which material? Against which alternative you already use?

It already happened. In 2024, researchers extracted over 2,700 real credentials — API keys, passwords, access tokens — from GitHub's AI, which had learned them during training and suggested them to other developers. When model improvement is on, your inputs may be used to improve the product. Turning model improvement off is a controllable setting, and it should be checked before any sensitive work.
How your tools handle your data

contentBlocks.content: The security question is not "is AI safe?" It's "what's the data, what are the settings, and what does my organization allow?"
For a staffer, safety is a toggle. For you, safety is a policy: which tools your people may use, and how you find out when they use something else.

genericSections.title: Distill - Caltrans

contentBlocks.label: Distill
contentBlocks.content:
ROLE
You are helping a Caltrans executive prepare a leadership briefing.

INSTRUCTION
Read this report and distill it for a leader who has no GTFS background
and needs to speak to it credibly:
https://reports.dds.dot.ca.gov/gtfs_schedule/2026/01/4/index.html

EXAMPLES
"Realtime completeness dropped mid-month" becomes "riders got less
accurate arrival times for part of January."

CONSTRAINTS
Translate technical findings into service impact.
Use only what the page states — no field names, examples, or
explanations it does not contain.
Maximum 400 words.

OUTPUT
Bottom Line — 2 sentences
Service Snapshot — 6 figures maximum
Compliance Status — what passed, what failed, what changed
What Actually Matters — which issues affect riders, which are
  housekeeping, and why
What I'd Ask — 3 questions for the team responsible
What I Couldn't See — anything you could not access or read: images,
  charts, tables, embedded content, sections that did not load

genericSections.goalText: Take a large amount of information and make it more consumable
